pos: adv. (certainly, without fail; in the Authorized Version the marker of a divine oath, and the first word the serpent contradicted)
etymology: From sure (Old French sur, from Latin securus, free from care) plus -ly. In the Old Testament it very often renders not an adverb at all but a Hebrew emphatic construction — the infinitive doubled with its own verb, which English can only carry by adding a word.
biblical_def: Surely is the Authorized Version's way of rendering a Hebrew emphasis that has no English equivalent: the verb is written twice, once as an infinitive and once as a finite form, and the effect is to place the whole weight of the speaker behind the statement. Hence the first threat in Scripture: “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” (Gen 2:17) — literally dying thou shalt die. And hence the first lie in Scripture is built by inserting one word into it: “Ye shall not surely die” (Gen 3:4). The serpent does not deny God's existence or His authorship of the command; he denies the certainty of the sanction, and every temptation since has been assembled the same way. Elsewhere the word marks the oath of judgment — “Surely none of the men that came up out of Egypt… shall see the land” (Num 32:11) — and the oath of grace, which is where Scripture ends: “Surely I come quickly” (Rev 22:20). Jacob's waking at Bethel gives the word its most human use: “Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines surely as certainly, undoubtedly, without doubt — and notes its use to affirm a thing firmly, as in the divine asseverations of Scripture.
webster_full: SURELY, adv. Certainly; undoubtedly; firmly.
He that createth all things, surely he is God.
2. Firmly; without danger of falling. He that walketh uprightly, walketh surely. Prov. x.
Note. In the Scriptures it frequently renders the Hebrew idiom in which the verb is doubled for emphasis, as, dying thou shalt die.
scriptures: Gen 2:17
But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.
Gen 3:4
And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die:

Surely none of the men that came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob; because they have not wholly followed me:
And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
corruption_summary: The oldest attack on Scripture is not the denial of God but the softening of His sanction — and it is still made by adding a single qualifying word to a plain threat.
corruption_paragraphs: Gen 3:4 is the model of every subsequent corruption of the word of God, and its method is worth naming exactly. The serpent grants the command, grants the Commander, and negates only the certainty: ye shall not surely die. He follows it with a motive — God is withholding something good — and the woman, who had already added a clause of her own to the prohibition, acts. Nothing in the exchange is crude. It is a hermeneutic, and it is the same one at work wherever hell is quietly reduced to a metaphor, wherever a plain command is called culturally conditioned, wherever the certainty of judgment becomes a possibility to be weighed.

The remedy is not to shout the threats but to notice that God binds Himself with the same word. Surely is the vocabulary of the divine oath, and Heb 6:17-18 says why God swears at all: to show the heirs of promise the immutability of His counsel, so that by two immutable things the believer might have strong consolation. The same certainty that makes Gen 2:17 terrible makes Rev 22:20 sweet. A God whose threats can be softened has promises that can be softened too, and the man who talks himself out of the first has lost the second in the same breath.
roots_summary: English sure from Latin securus; rendering the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction (verb doubled for emphasis) and Greek particles of asseveration such as nai and men.
roots_lines: Hebrew infinitive absolute — the verb written twice, as moth tamuth (Gen 2:17), literally “dying thou shalt die”; the KJV renders the doubling with surely.
Gen 3:4 in Hebrew — lo moth temuthun, the same doubled construction with a negative laid across it; the serpent quotes the grammar and reverses the verdict.
Hebrew aken (H403) — surely, truly; Jacob's word at Bethel, “Surely the LORD is in this place” (Gen 28:16).
Hebrew im in oath formulas — “Surely none of the men…” (Num 32:11) is an elliptical oath: if they shall see the land, with the curse left unspoken.
Greek nai (G3483) — yea, surely; nai, erchomai tachu, “Surely I come quickly” (Rev 22:20).
usage: “Thou shalt surely die” — the Hebrew doubling, the whole weight of God behind a sanction.
“Ye shall not surely die” — the first lie, made by qualifying a certainty.
“Surely I come quickly” — the same oath-word, turned toward comfort.

pos: adj. (fixed, established, not to be doubted; also, in the Authorized Version's older idiom, a certain man — a particular but unnamed person)
etymology: From Old French certain, from Latin certus, settled, decided — the past participle of cernere, to sift or to decide. What is certain has been sifted and the question closed.
biblical_def: Certain carries two distinct senses in the Authorized Version, and English has kept only one of them. The first is the modern sense of established beyond doubt: the Law requires that a capital charge be enquired into “diligently, and, behold, it be true, and the thing certain” (Deu 17:4) — a man's life may not turn on a probable accusation. Paul uses the same sense to strip the rich of their illusions: “we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out” (1Ti 6:7). And Hebrews uses it for the one prospect the impenitent cannot avoid: “a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation” (Heb 10:27). The second sense is the older English indefinite — a certain man, meaning a particular man whose name is not given. This is how nearly every parable begins: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luk 10:30). The idiom is not vagueness. It signals a real, specific, individual man whom the hearer is not permitted to identify with anyone but himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines certain first as sure, true, undoubted, and secondly as particular but not named — the sense in which the Scriptures speak of a certain man or a certain city.
webster_full: CERTAIN, a. Sure; true; undoubted; unquestionable; that cannot be denied.
2. Assured in mind; having no doubts.
3. Unfailing; always producing the intended effect; as a certain remedy.
4. Particular. There came a certain poor widow. Mark xii.
Note. In this last sense it denotes a particular person or thing not named or described.
scriptures: Deu 17:4
And it be told thee, and thou hast heard of it, and enquired diligently, and, behold, it be true, and the thing certain, that such abomination is wrought in Israel:
For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.
And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
corruption_summary: Certainty itself is treated as a moral defect — humility redefined as permanent tentativeness — while Scripture makes assurance a duty and a comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: A settled current in modern religious writing holds that confident conviction is arrogance and that the mature believer holds everything loosely. Scripture does not know this virtue. Luke wrote his Gospel expressly so that Theophilus “mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4); Paul says “I know whom I have believed” (2Ti 1:12); John wrote his epistle “that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1Jn 5:13). The LBCF devotes a whole chapter to assurance and calls it attainable. Genuine humility is not doubt about what God has said; it is submission to it.

The doubt-as-virtue posture also gets the moral risk backwards. Deu 17:4 shows Scripture's actual concern about certainty: not that men are too sure of God's word, but that they are too ready to act on an unexamined report about their neighbour. The Law demands diligent enquiry before a charge is treated as certain, precisely because certainty has consequences. Be slow to be sure about a man; do not be slow to be sure about God.
roots_summary: Latin certus, decided, from cernere, to sift; rendering Hebrew kun (H3559), to be established, and Greek tis (G5100), a certain one, the indefinite pronoun.
roots_lines: Latin certus — sifted, decided; from cernere, to separate, the root also of discern and concern.
Hebrew nakon (H3559) — established, fixed; “the thing certain” in Deu 17:4, a charge that has stood examination.
Hebrew yatsib (H3330) — sure, certain; used in Daniel of a dream whose interpretation is trustworthy (Dan 2:45).
Greek tis (G5100) — a certain one, someone; the indefinite pronoun that opens most parables, “a certain man”.
Greek asphaleia (G803) — certainty, safety, literally not-slipping; Luke's stated purpose in writing (Luk 1:4).
usage: “The thing certain” — a charge that has survived diligent enquiry.
“It is certain we can carry nothing out” — the fact every estate plan concedes.
“A certain man” — not vagueness, but a particular man the hearer must not identify with anyone else.

pos: adj. (firm, stable, not liable to fail; in Scripture said of God's foundation, God's testimony, and the believer's hope)
etymology: From Old French sur, from Latin securus — se- (without) plus cura (care), that is, free from anxiety. English kept the outward sense of firmness; the Latin root remembers the inward sense of a mind at rest, and Scripture joins the two.
biblical_def: Sure in the Authorized Version is a load-bearing word: it describes what will hold when weight is put on it. It is said of the foundation: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16), the prophecy Peter and Paul both apply to Christ; and again, “the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19) — a verse that grounds the perseverance of the saints in God's knowledge rather than in the believer's grip. It is said of the Scriptures: “the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7) — sure enough that a simple man may build on it without a scholar's help. And it is said of hope: “which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil” (Heb 6:19) — an anchor thrown not downward into the seabed but upward into the holy of holies, where Christ has already gone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sure as certain, unfailing, infallible — and also as firm, stable, secure, not liable to failure, loss or change.
webster_full: SURE, a. Certain; unfailing; infallible.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy. 2 Pet. i.
2. Certainly knowing, or having full confidence. I am sure that ye are not of us.
3. Firm; stable; steady; not liable to failure, loss or change.
4. Safe; being in no danger. Fear not, thou art sure.
scriptures: Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Heb 6:19
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
corruption_summary: 2Ti 2:19 is quoted for comfort while its second half is dropped, producing an assurance detached from the departing-from-iniquity that Paul makes its companion seal.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul stamps the foundation with two inscriptions, not one. The first is God's side: The Lord knoweth them that are his — election, and therefore a security no failure of the believer's memory or nerve can undo. The second is the believer's side: Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. Quote the first alone and you get the bare once-saved-always-saved slogan the dictionary rejects; quote the second alone and you get a religion of self-watching. The Reformed doctrine is perseverance, which holds both: God preserves His own, and the mark that He is doing so is that they depart from iniquity.

Psa 19:7 answers the parallel corruption about Scripture. The testimony of the LORD is sure, and its effect is to make the simple wise — not the trained, not the credentialed, the simple. The doctrine of perspicuity stands on verses like this one: the plain man with a plain Bible may know what he must know for salvation and obedience. That is why the Reformers put the text in the common tongue, and why any scheme requiring the layman to wait on the expert before he may be sure of anything is a step back toward the darkness they left.
roots_summary: Latin securus, free from care; rendering Hebrew aman (H539), to be firm or faithful — the root of amen — and Greek bebaios (G949), firm, and stereos (G4731), solid.
roots_lines: Latin securus — se- without + cura care; the same root gives English secure.
Hebrew aman (H539) — to support, be firm, be faithful; the root behind amen, and behind “the testimony of the LORD is sure” (Psa 19:7).
Hebrew musad musad — “a sure foundation” in Isa 28:16 is a doubled participle: founded, founded — a foundation that has been laid and laid firmly.
Greek bebaios (G949) — firm, steadfast; the anchor “sure and stedfast” of Heb 6:19.
Greek stereos (G4731) — solid, hard; “the foundation of God standeth sure” (2Ti 2:19), the word behind English stereo in its old sense of solidity.
usage: “The foundation of God standeth sure” — sealed on both sides, God's knowing and the believer's departing.
“A sure foundation” — a stone laid and laid firmly, applied by the apostles to Christ.
“An anchor of the soul… sure and stedfast” — thrown upward, within the veil.

pos: adv. (in deed, in fact, in reality; the Authorized Version's word for the genuine article as against the nominal one)
etymology: Originally two words, in deed — that is, in act, as opposed to in word or in appearance. English fused them, and in fusing them nearly lost the contrast that gives the word its point.
biblical_def: Indeed distinguishes the real thing from the thing merely called by the name, and the New Testament uses it at some of its sharpest turns. Of freedom: “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36) — spoken to men who had just insisted they were never in bondage to any man, and who were at that moment slaves of sin. Of discipleship: “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31) — continuance, not initial profession, is what makes a disciple the real article. Of the Baptist: the chief priests dared not deny that “all men counted John, that he was a prophet indeed” (Mar 11:32) — and their fear of saying so out loud exposes them. In every case the word does the same work: it drives a wedge between the label and the substance, and it asks the reader which side of the wedge he is on. Nathanael receives the Lord's own use of it: “an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indeed as in reality, in truth, in fact — and notes its use to denote concession, admission, or emphasis according to the sense.
webster_full: INDEED, adv. [in and deed, in fact.] In reality; in truth; in fact.
The carnal mind is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. Rom. viii.
2. It is used to denote concession or admission; as, ye are indeed learned, but not wise.
3. It is used to note interrogation with surprise; as, is it indeed so?
scriptures: Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Joh 8:31
Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;
But if we shall say, Of men; they feared the people: for all men counted John, that he was a prophet indeed.
Deu 17:4
And it be told thee, and thou hast heard of it, and enquired diligently, and, behold, it be true, and the thing certain, that such abomination is wrought in Israel:
corruption_summary: Joh 8:36 is quoted for a freedom the passage explicitly denies — autonomy — when the freedom Christ names is freedom from the servitude of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: “Free indeed” is among the most misappropriated phrases in Scripture, printed over sentiments about self-determination and being true to oneself. The context is unambiguous: “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin” (Joh 8:34), and the freedom offered is release from that bondage into the household of the Son. Nothing in the passage promises freedom from law, from authority, or from constraint. The men Christ is addressing believed themselves free already, which is exactly the condition the word indeed is inserted to puncture.

Joh 8:31 supplies the test the modern church most needs and least applies. Those addressed are described as having believed on Him, and the Lord immediately attaches a condition to the reality of their discipleship: if ye continue in my word. Continuance is the evidence, not the cause — but where there is no continuance, the New Testament does not encourage the profession to be treated as a disciple indeed. That is the doctrine of perseverance stated as a pastoral test, and it stands against the decisionism that counts a raised hand as a settled matter.
roots_summary: English in deed, in act; rendering Greek ontos (G3689), really, from the participle of eimi, to be, and alethos (G230), truly.
roots_lines: English in deed — in act, as opposed to in name or in word; the two words fused in Middle English.
Greek ontos (G3689) — really, actually; from on, the participle of eimi, to be. “Free indeed” is ontos eleutheroi — free in the order of being.
Greek alethos (G230) — truly, of a truth; “disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31) and “an Israelite indeed” (Joh 1:47).
Greek men — the concessive particle, often rendered “indeed” where a contrast with de follows: “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mat 26:41).
1Ti 5:3, 5 — “a widow indeed”, ontos chera, distinguishing the genuinely destitute widow from the one with family to keep her.
usage: “Free indeed” — freedom from the servitude of sin, not freedom from authority.
“Disciples indeed” — continuance in His word is what makes the profession real.
“A prophet indeed” — what the priests knew and would not say aloud.

pos: adv. (for what cause or reason; in Scripture the word of lament, of rebuke, and of the cry from the cross)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hwi, the instrumental case of hwa, who — literally by what. It belongs to the same family as what, when, where, and how.
biblical_def: Why is the word Scripture gives to the sufferer, and it is remarkable how freely it is given. The Psalter is full of it, and the twenty-second Psalm opens with the sharpest instance in the Bible: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?” (Psa 22:1). This is not the complaint of unbelief — the sufferer says my God twice — and it is the sentence the Lord Jesus takes on His own lips at the ninth hour: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mat 27:46; Mar 15:34). The Son of God asks why in the dark, and in doing so sanctifies the question for every believer who has ever had to ask it. But why is also the word of rebuke: “If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?” (Joh 18:23) — the Lord before the high priest, refusing to accept an injustice silently, which is worth noting against the sentimental view that meekness never questions.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines why as an adverb of interrogation, for what cause or reason, and notes its use also as an expression of surprise or of remonstrance.
webster_full: WHY, adv. For what cause or reason, interrogatively.
Why is his chariot so long in coming? Judges v.
2. For which reason or cause, relatively. This is the reason why he came.
3. It is used sometimes emphatically, or in familiar language, as an expression of surprise or of remonstrance.
scriptures: Psa 22:1
To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?
corruption_summary: The cry of dereliction is emptied by two opposite errors: the claim that the Father actually broke fellowship with the Son, and the claim that Christ was merely reciting a psalm.
corruption_paragraphs: Some popular preaching says the Father turned away from the Son in disgust, or that the Trinity was in some sense ruptured at the cross. That cannot be. The Persons of the Godhead are one in essence and inseparable in operation, and the Son is never less than the beloved Son. What the cry reports is real and it is judicial: the Son bears the penalty of the elect's sin, and with it the withdrawal of the felt comfort and favourable presence that the sin deserved. Penal substitution requires that the forsaking be genuine; divine simplicity requires that it not be a division in God. Both stand.

The opposite error treats the cry as a devotional recitation — Christ quoting Psalm 22 to point His hearers to a psalm that ends in triumph, and therefore not really in anguish. He is indeed quoting it, and the psalm does end in triumph, and the whole psalm is prophecy fulfilled in front of the reader: the pierced hands and feet, the parted garments, the cast lots. But a quotation cried with a loud voice at the ninth hour by a man three hours in darkness is not a literary reference. He asks why, in the dark, and the answer is written across the New Testament: for us.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon hwi, by what; rendering Hebrew lammah (H4100 with the preposition), to what purpose, and Greek hina ti and dia ti, for what.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon hwi — the instrumental of hwa, who; literally “by what”.
Hebrew lammah (H4100) — why, to what end; the opening word of Psa 22:1 and the commonest why of the Psalter.
Hebrew maddua (H4069) — why, from mah + yada: literally “what is known”, that is, on what grounds.
Aramaic lema sabachthani — the actual words from the cross, preserved untranslated by Matthew and Mark before they give the Greek.
Greek hina ti — “to what end”; the Septuagint's rendering of lammah, and the form quoted at Mat 27:46.
usage: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” — the question asked in the dark by the Son of God.
“Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” — the believer permitted to interrogate his own despondency.
“Why smitest thou me?” — meekness that does not accept injustice in silence.

pos: conj. (introducing the first of two alternatives; in Scripture the word that binds a believer to God in either outcome)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hwaether, which of two — the comparative of the hwa (who) stem, exactly parallel to either and other. It was once a pronoun meaning which of the two, and only later a conjunction.
biblical_def: The New Testament's most striking use of whether is not to raise a doubt but to dissolve one, by declaring that both branches of the alternative land in the same place. “For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's” (Rom 14:8) — the two outcomes a man fears most are set side by side and both are annexed to Christ. Paul does the same with the smallest things: “Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31), so that no act is too ordinary to have a Godward direction. And he does it with his own reputation, refusing to be troubled by the motives of rival preachers: “whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice” (Php 1:18). The word also governs the duty of testing: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — here the alternative is real, and the believer is commanded to decide it rather than to hold it open.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives whether as a pronoun signifying which of two, and as a conjunction introducing the first of two alternatives, the second following with or.
webster_full: WHETHER, pron. Which of two.
Whether of them twain did the will of his father? Matt. xxi.
WHETHER, conj. Used to introduce the first of two or more alternatives, the last being introduced by or.
Note. From the Saxon hwaether, formed on the stem of who, as either and other are formed.
scriptures: Rom 14:8
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Php 1:18
What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.
corruption_summary: Php 1:18 is used to license indifference about who preaches and what they preach, when Paul is speaking of impure motives and elsewhere anathematises a false gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: “Whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached” is regularly produced to silence any criticism of a popular ministry. But the alternative Paul allows is about motive — men preaching Christ out of envy and strife, hoping to add affliction to his bonds — and he is saying that God will use a true message even from a rotten heart. He is not indifferent to the message itself. The same apostle writes, in the same volume of Scripture, that if any man preach another gospel “let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8-9). Php 1:18 covers a bad preacher of the true gospel; it has nothing to say for a preacher of a false one.

1Jn 4:1 gives the balancing command and it is not optional: try the spirits. The apostolic assumption is that many false prophets are already out in the world and that ordinary believers are competent and obliged to test what they hear, by the apostolic doctrine of Christ come in the flesh. Discernment is not a suspicious temperament; it is obedience. And Rom 14:8 explains why a Christian can afford to be fearless in exercising it: the two outcomes he might risk, living and dying, both belong to his Lord already.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon hwaether, which of two; rendering Hebrew disjunctive constructions with im and Greek eite…eite, whether…or, and ei in indirect questions.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon hwaether — which of two; formed on the who stem exactly as either and other are formed.
Greek eite…eite — whether…or; the paired conjunction of Rom 14:8 and 1Co 10:31, setting two alternatives under one verdict.
Greek ei (G1487) — if, whether; introducing an indirect question, as at 1Jn 4:1.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, prove, as metal is assayed; the verb of “try the spirits”.
Hebrew im (H518) — if, whether; in disjunctive questions, “Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?” (Josh 5:13).
usage: “Whether we live… whether we die” — both branches annexed to Christ, so neither is to be feared.
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink” — no act too ordinary to have a Godward direction.
“Try the spirits whether they are of God” — an alternative the believer is commanded to decide, not to hold open.

pos: adv. and conj. (otherwise; besides; in Scripture chiefly in the divine formula there is none else)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon elles, otherwise — a genitive form of a lost adjective meaning other, cognate with Latin alius. The same root gives alien and alias.
biblical_def: Else reaches its height in Isaiah, where it becomes the vocabulary of monotheism. God says it of Himself, again and again, and each time it excludes not merely rival worship but rival existence: “I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me” (Isa 45:5). That last clause is addressed to Cyrus, a pagan king who did not know the God who was arming him — so the sovereignty asserted extends over rulers who have never heard of it. The same chapter turns the exclusion into an invitation: “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else” (Isa 45:22) — the verse under which Charles Spurgeon was converted in a Colchester snowstorm. In other places else marks the fork in a road: “either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). There is no third option in view. The word's whole work is to close off alternatives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines else as otherwise, in the other case, or besides — noting that it excludes all but the thing named.
webster_full: ELSE, a. or pron. Other; one or something beside; as, who else is coming?
ELSE, adv. Otherwise; in the other case; if the fact were different.
Repent, or else I will come unto thee quickly. Rev. ii.
2. Beside; except that mentioned; as, nowhere else.
Note. From the Saxon elles, otherwise, of the same root with the Latin alius.
scriptures: Isa 45:5
I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:
Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: The exclusivity of Isaiah's none else is treated as ancient Israelite polemic rather than a truth claim, and religious pluralism supplies a tolerance Scripture nowhere offers.
corruption_paragraphs: The pluralist reading holds that Isaiah 45 records one nation's devotional preference for its own deity, and that a mature faith today will hear it as poetry rather than as a claim about what exists. The chapter forecloses that. The God speaking claims to have raised up a Persian king by name before he was born, to form light and create darkness, and to be the only Saviour there is — and He addresses these claims to the ends of the earth, not to Israel alone. A statement designed from the outset to include every nation cannot be reduced to one nation's house style.

Mat 6:24 applies the same exclusivity to the heart. The Lord does not warn against loving money too much; He says no man can serve two masters, and that the attempt always resolves into hating one. Modern discipleship talk that speaks of balancing priorities has quietly denied the sentence. And Isa 45:22 shows why the exclusivity is good news rather than bad: because there is none else, the invitation can be issued to the ends of the earth without qualification. A God who were one option among several could save only some; a God beside whom there is none else can say look unto me, and be ye saved, and mean everyone who looks.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon elles, otherwise, cognate with Latin alius; rendering Hebrew od (H5750), yet, still, in the formula en od, there is no more, and Greek ei de me, but if not.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon elles — otherwise; from the same Indo-European root as Latin alius, other, whence alien and alias.
Hebrew en od — literally “there is not yet”, that is, there is no other; the refrain of Isa 45:5, 6, 14, 18, 21, 22.
Hebrew zulah (H2108) — besides, except; “there is no God beside me” (Isa 45:5).
Greek ei de me — “but if not”, rendered or else; the alternative branch in Mat 6:24 and Luk 16:13.
Greek allos (G243) — other, another of the same kind; the Greek cousin of Latin alius and of English else.
usage: “I am the LORD, and there is none else” — a claim about what exists, not a preference.
“Look unto me, and be ye saved… there is none else” — exclusivity is what makes the offer universal.
“Or else he will hold to the one” — no third road between God and mammon.

pos: v. (the negative of can; in Scripture the word that marks a real moral inability, not a mere difficulty)
etymology: A fusion of can and not, written as two words into the eighteenth century and as one thereafter. The Authorized Version prints it both ways.
biblical_def: Cannot is one of the most doctrinally weighted words in the New Testament, because Scripture repeatedly says of fallen man not that he will not but that he cannot. “They that are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom 8:8), which follows from the verse before it: the carnal mind is enmity against God, is not subject to His law, “neither indeed can be”. “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1Co 15:50) — the body as it now is, mortal and corruptible, is unfit for the world to come and must be changed. “As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me” (Joh 15:4). And “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24), where the impossibility is not of effort but of nature: two absolute masters cannot both be absolute. In every case the inability is moral, not physical — the sinner is not prevented by a chain but disinclined by a nature, which is why he is fully responsible for what he cannot do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats cannot as the compound of can and not, expressing want of power or of ability, and notes that it is written as one word or as two.
webster_full: CANNOT. This word is usually written as one word, but is properly two, can and not, expressing inability.
CAN, v.i. To be able; to have sufficient strength, means or moral power.
Note. The distinction between natural and moral inability is of great moment in theology; a man cannot fly, and a man cannot love what he hates, but not in the same manner.
Note. How can ye, being evil, speak good things? Matt. xii.
scriptures: Rom 8:8
So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.
Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption.
Joh 15:4
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: The Bible's cannot is softened into finds it difficult, which quietly denies total depravity and makes regeneration an assistance rather than a resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: Almost every departure from Reformed soteriology can be traced to the handling of this one word. Semi-Pelagian and Arminian schemes must read cannot as a strong will not, leaving the fallen will with enough residual power to cooperate with grace. Scripture will not bend that way. Paul writes that the carnal mind “is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7), and John reports the Lord saying “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). Total depravity does not mean men are as wicked as they could be; it means the whole man — mind, affections, will — is fallen, and that the disability reaches the very faculty that would have to choose.

The old distinction preserves both truths. A man's inability is moral, not natural: he is not shackled, he is disinclined; he has every faculty required to come to Christ and no desire to use them. That is why the inability excuses no one — a man who cannot love what he hates is not thereby innocent — and why the remedy must be a new nature rather than better arguments. Eze 36:26 promises a new heart, and Eph 2:5 says God quickened us when we were dead. Not helped; quickened. The cannot of Rom 8:8 is what makes monergism necessary and what makes it glorious.
roots_summary: English can + not; rendering Greek ou dunamai (G3756 with G1410), not to be able, and Hebrew lo yakol, he is not able.
roots_lines: Greek ou dunamai — not to be able; the flat negative of power, used at Rom 8:8, Joh 15:4, and 1Co 15:50.
Greek oude dunatai — “neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7); the added oude forecloses the possibility as well as the fact.
Hebrew lo yakol — he is not able; used of Joseph's brethren, who “could not speak peaceably unto him” (Gen 37:4) — a moral inability if ever there was one.
Joh 6:44 — oudeis dunatai elthein, “no man can come to me”; the drawing of the Father is the necessary condition.
Eph 2:1, 5 — nekrous, dead; the state that makes the cannot intelligible and the quickening necessary.
usage: “They that are in the flesh cannot please God” — inability of nature, not of opportunity.
“Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom” — the mortal body must be changed, not merely improved.
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon” — two absolute masters cannot both be absolute.

pos: adj. and n. (sufficient; as much as is required — and in Scripture, the confession the covetous heart never makes)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon genoh, sufficient, from a root meaning to attain or to reach. The word originally described arriving at a required measure, not an abundance beyond it.
biblical_def: Enough in Scripture is a matter of the heart rather than the ledger. Esau, reconciled to his brother and offered a present, says the words the covetous cannot say: “I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself” (Gen 33:9). At the building of the tabernacle the people bring so much that the workmen have to be restrained — “the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much” (Exo 36:7) — the only recorded instance in Scripture of a building fund being closed for excess of giving. Proverbs names the opposite condition with a memorable image: “The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough” (Pro 30:15). And the prodigal's turning point is an act of arithmetic about enough: “How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!” (Luk 15:17). He comes to himself by remembering a house where there was enough, and the road home begins there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines enough as that which satisfies desire, or gives content; sufficient; equal to the powers or abilities — and notes it as both adjective and noun.
webster_full: ENOUGH, a. That satisfies desire, or gives content; that may answer the purpose; sufficient.
ENOUGH, n. A sufficiency; a quantity of a thing which satisfies desire, or is adequate to the wants.
I have enough, my brother. Gen. xxxiii.
ENOUGH, adv. Sufficiently; in a quantity or degree that satisfies.
Note. From the Saxon genoh, sufficient; the primary sense is to reach or attain.
scriptures: Gen 33:9
And Esau said, I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself.
Exo 36:7
For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much.
The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough:
And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel makes more the standing evidence of God's favour, so that a Christian is taught never to say enough and to read contentment as small faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Where increase is preached as the reliable sign of blessing, the horseleach of Pro 30:15 is installed in the pulpit. The seed-faith appeal works precisely by ensuring that no giver ever arrives at enough: the offering is always a deposit against a larger return, so the appetite is fed rather than mortified. Scripture's pattern in Exo 36:7 is the exact reverse — a collection stopped by proclamation because the people had brought too much. It is worth asking when a modern ministry last restrained its own giving.

Against this stands the plain apostolic standard: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8), and “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1Ti 6:6). Enough is not a low ambition; it is the floor from which generosity becomes possible, since a man who has enough has something to give. And Luk 15:17 shows the doctrine at its most pastoral. The prodigal does not repent because he calculates a better return; he repents because he remembers a father's house where the hired servants had bread enough and to spare. The memory of sufficiency in the father's house is what turns him around, and it is the same memory that turns any sinner around.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon genoh, sufficient; rendering Hebrew rab (H7227), much, enough, and day (H1767), sufficiency, and Greek arkeo (G714), to suffice, and perisseuo (G4052), to abound.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon genoh — sufficient; from a root meaning to reach or attain a required measure.
Hebrew rab (H7227) — much, many, enough; Esau's “I have enough” (Gen 33:9) is yesh li rab, “I have much”.
Hebrew day (H1767) — sufficiency; the root behind El Shaddai in one traditional derivation, God the all-sufficient.
Hebrew hon in Pro 30:15 — the four things that “say not, It is enough”: the grave, the barren womb, the earth, and the fire.
Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, have over and above; “bread enough and to spare” (Luk 15:17).
usage: “I have enough, my brother” — the sentence a covetous heart cannot form.
“Sufficient for all the work… and too much” — the one collection Scripture records being closed.
“Say not, It is enough” — the grave, the womb, the earth, and the fire; and the covetous man among them.

pos: adv. (in truth, verily; the Authorized Version's word for a confession wrung out by evidence)
etymology: From true (Anglo-Saxon treowe, faithful) plus -ly. In the Gospels it frequently renders the same Greek word that elsewhere becomes verily, and in the Hebrew it often stands for a particle of asseveration at the head of a sentence.
biblical_def: Truly in the Authorized Version is very often the word of a man forced to a conclusion he did not begin with. The centurion at the cross has watched an execution he had no reason to think remarkable, and then: “when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mar 15:39). A Roman soldier, at the foot of a Roman cross, gives the confession the Sanhedrin would not. Asaph reaches his truly the other way, after a long struggle with the prosperity of the wicked, and puts the conclusion first: “Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart” (Psa 73:1) — the psalm then narrates how nearly he lost it. Elsewhere the word simply weighs one thing against another: “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37); “John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence” (Act 1:5). In each pairing the first clause is granted so that the second may land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines truly as in truth, according to fact, without deceit; and also as really, in fact, and in the way of confirmation.
webster_full: TRULY, adv. In truth; according to truth; in accordance with fact.
2. Really; without deceit or fraud; honestly.
3. In fact; in reality; as, truly this was the Son of God.
4. Exactly; justly; as, to measure truly.
Note. It answers in many places to the verily of the same version.
scriptures: And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God.
Psa 73:1
A Psalm of Asaph. Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Act 1:5
For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.
corruption_summary: The centurion's confession is downgraded to “a son of God” or to admiration for a brave death, and Psalm 73 is read as a crisis of faith that ends in acceptance rather than in sight.
corruption_paragraphs: A long line of critical commentary renders the centurion's words as “truly this man was a son of God”, meaning a hero or a righteous man in the Roman idiom, and treats Mark as recording pagan admiration rather than confession. That reading has to work against the whole architecture of Mark, whose first verse announces “the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God”, and whose narrative withholds any human confession of that title until this moment. Mark has been building to a Gentile at the cross, and the veil torn in the previous verse is his commentary on it.

Psalm 73 is likewise flattened when it is read as a story about learning to live with unanswered questions. Asaph does not learn to tolerate the prosperity of the wicked; he goes into the sanctuary of God and understands their end (Psa 73:17), and comes out with a settled verdict about slippery places and a settled desire — “whom have I in heaven but thee?” His truly is not a brave posture adopted in the dark. It is the report of a man who was given light, and it is placed at the head of the psalm so the reader knows where the road ends before he walks it.
roots_summary: English true + -ly; rendering Greek alethos (G230), truly, and amen (G281) in some places, and Hebrew ak (H389), surely, only, at the head of a clause.
roots_lines: Greek alethos (G230) — truly, really; the centurion's word in Mar 15:39 and Mat 27:54.
Greek amen (G281) — the Hebrew asseveration carried over untranslated; rendered verily in the Gospels and occasionally truly.
Greek men — the concessive particle, “on the one hand”; the KJV often renders it truly where a but follows, as at Mat 9:37 and Act 1:5.
Hebrew ak (H389) — surely, only; the emphatic opening of Psa 73:1.
Hebrew emet (H571) — truth, firmness, from aman, to support; the same root as amen.
usage: “Truly this man was the Son of God” — a Roman soldier confessing what the council would not.
“Truly God is good to Israel” — the verdict placed first, before the struggle is narrated.
“The harvest truly is plenteous” — the first clause granted so the second may land.
